[THOUGHT] Age is essential to narrow the differential (atopic dermatitis common in younger, seborrheic in adults, rosacea in middle-aged, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma in older adults). I need the patient's age before asking distribution or appearance details.

[QUERY] How old are you?

[THOUGHT] The differential includes chronic dermatoses such as seborrheic dermatitis, chronic contact/atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, or cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma. The next critical piece of information is the morphology of the lesions (scaling type, plaques vs papules, lichenification, oozing) because that strongly narrows the diagnosis. I'll ask one focused question about how the rash looks. 

[QUERY] What do the lesions look like—are they red scaly patches or raised plaques, greasy yellow flakes, small bumps, blisters, or thickened/lichenified skin? Any oozing, crusting, or scale?

[REFERENCE] 2. The patient reports a year-long history of an itchy rash on his upper body and face.
[REFERENCE] 7. Hypopigmented macules around the elbows.

[RESPONSE] I have an itchy rash on my upper body and face, and I also have hypopigmented macules around my elbows.

[THOUGHT] Key differential includes seborrheic dermatitis, chronic eczema/atopic dermatitis, tinea versicolor, psoriasis, and cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides). Knowing prior treatments and response will help distinguish fungal causes (respond to antifungals), inflammatory dermatoses (improve with topical steroids/emollients), or refractory disease suggesting CTCL (poor or transient response to steroids). I will ask one focused question about treatments and response.

[QUERY] Have you used any treatments for the rash (topical corticosteroids, antifungal shampoos/creams, emollients, oral medications, or others), and if so did the rash improve, worsen, or stay the same?

[REFERENCE] N/A
[RESPONSE] I'm not sure — I don't recall using any treatments for the rash.

[THOUGHT] Exact distribution (specific face regions and upper trunk areas) will strongly narrow the differential (seborrheic dermatitis favors scalp/eyebrows/nasolabial folds/chest; tinea versicolor favors upper trunk; mycosis fungoides often in sun-protected trunk/limbs). I need this single focused location detail before ordering tests.

[QUERY] Exactly where are the lesions on your face and upper body—please list specific sites (scalp, eyebrows, forehead, around the nose/nasolabial folds, cheeks, chest, upper back, shoulders, etc.) and say whether they are on one or both sides.

[REFERENCE] 2. The patient reports a year-long history of an itchy rash on his upper body and face.
[REFERENCE] 5. Thinning of the eyebrows.

[RESPONSE] The lesions are on the face and upper body, and there is thinning of the eyebrows. The information provided does not state whether these findings are on one side or both sides.

[THOUGHT] I need to distinguish seborrheic dermatitis (greasy yellow scaling on scalp/eyebrows/nasolabial folds) from other causes (tinea versicolor, cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma). Presence of greasy, yellowish scales on the eyebrows or scalp would strongly support seborrheic dermatitis. I'll ask one focused question about scaling on those sites.

[QUERY] Do you have greasy, yellowish scales or flaking on your scalp or eyebrows?

[REFERENCE] N/A
[RESPONSE] I'm not sure — I don't recall having greasy, yellowish scales or flaking on my scalp or eyebrows.

[THOUGHT] A chronic, itchy year-long rash involving face and upper trunk with eyebrow thinning and hypopigmented macules raises concern for cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides) among other chronic dermatoses. Definitive differentiation requires histology and immunophenotyping. The next critical step is tissue diagnosis rather than further history alone.

[TEST] Perform a punch skin biopsy of an active lesion (preferably from an upper trunk or a hypopigmented patch) with histopathology and immunohistochemistry (including CD3, CD4, CD8, CD7; request T‑cell clonality studies if available).

1. Skin biopsy findings: Chronic inflammatory cells with features suggestive of leprosy.
2. Nerve conduction studies findings: Reduced sensory nerve action potentials in the ulnar nerves.
3. Anti-PGL-1_antibodies: Positive.
8. Skin examination observation: Multiple erythematous macules and papules on the face, arms, chest, and back.
9. Insensitivity to light touch around the hypopigmented areas.
10. Insensitivity to temperature around the hypopigmented areas.
11. Insensitivity to pinprick around the hypopigmented areas.
12. Slight reduction in grip strength bilaterally.

[THOUGHT] The combination of chronic inflammatory changes on skin biopsy consistent with leprosy, positive anti‑PGL‑1 antibodies, multiple erythematous macules/papules on face and trunk, eyebrow thinning (madarosis), symmetric sensory loss (light touch/temperature/pinprick) over hypopigmented patches, peripheral nerve dysfunction (reduced ulnar SNAPs and mild grip weakness) strongly supports Hansen disease. Positive PGL‑1 and diffuse facial involvement with madarosis point toward a multibacillary (lepromatous) form rather than tuberculoid disease. Therefore the single most likely diagnosis is lepromatous (multibacillary) leprosy. 

[DIAGNOSIS] Lepromatous (multibacillary) leprosy (Hansen disease).
